title: Wyandot Name: Kah-ten-tah-teh, Fair Land of Tomorrow
summary: Long before Filson popularized Dark and Bloody Ground, Wyandot hunters coming south of the Ohio called this country Kah-ten-tah-teh, Fair Land of Tomorrow.
bodyMarkdown:
Long before [John Filson](/people/#john-filson) and other writers made "Dark and Bloody Ground" famous, the nations who knew this country had their own names for it.

The [Wyandot](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wyandot_people) were an Iroquoian-speaking people. Their nation took shape around 1650 from survivors of the Huron confederacy and its neighbors after the Iroquois wars. By the 1700s their towns lay north of the Ohio, and their hunters came south across the valley, often along the [Warriors' Path](/stories/athiamiowee-the-warriors-path-through-kentucky/).

A [Forest Service history](https://www.npshistory.com/publications/usfs/region/8/daniel-boone/history/appa.htm) of the Daniel Boone National Forest records the Wyandot name for this land as Kah-ten-tah-teh. It is rendered "Fair Land of Tomorrow" or "Land Where We Will Live Tomorrow."

Other nations had other words. The same history gives a Shawnee name, Kain-tuck-ee, glossed "at the head of the river." It records Mohawk and Delaware forms like Kentucke, meaning "among the meadows" or "place of the meadows."

Where the English name "Kentucky" really comes from is still debated. Many linguists [lean toward an Iroquoian root](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kentucky) meaning "meadow" or "at the meadow." Some Iroquoian readings also give "land of tomorrow." The name was in European records by the 1750s and became the state's name in 1792.

"Dark and Bloody Ground" is a different matter. It is often credited to the Cherokee leader [Dragging Canoe](/people/#dragging-canoe), but no known Native word for the country means anything like that. It grew up in settler storytelling about the border wars.

What the names share matters more than which one won. Wyandot, Shawnee, Delaware, Cherokee, and others treated Kentucky as known and claimed hunting country, not empty land. Each gave it a name in its own language.

Wyandot warriors also fought on this ground. They joined the 1782 siege of [Bryan Station](/stories/bryan-station-siege-august-1782/) alongside [Simon Girty](/people/#simon-girty), and the wider story is told in [the Wyandot on Kentucky's northern frontier](/stories/wyandot-on-kentuckys-northern-frontier/).

## Kentucky today

The Wyandotte Nation, a federally recognized tribe, is based today in northeastern Oklahoma. In Kentucky, the old names live on in the state's own name and in Daniel Boone National Forest's histories of the land.
